opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the beginning I was pretty skeptical. When Yann first started talking about JEPA, the joint embedding predictive architecture, my reaction was: this sounds nice conceptually, but is it really different from what we've already been doing? We had contrastive learning, we had BYOL, DINO, all these joint-embedding methods, and on the other side we had masked autoencoders and generative pretraining. So JEPA felt a bit like a repackaging. And there was a practical worry too: if you predict in latent space instead of pixel space, how do you stop the whole thing from collapsing? With pixels, at least the target is grounded. You know what you're supposed to reconstruct.

I'd also worked on MAE-style approaches, so I had some intuition that reconstruction is a very strong signal. Part of me thought, why throw that away?

What changed my mind wasn't one paper. It was slowly realizing what the real question is. The question isn't "latent or pixel" as a technical trick. It's: what is a world model supposed to capture? If you insist on predicting every pixel, you spend huge capacity modeling things that don't matter, like the exact texture of leaves or the noise in a video frame. The world is fundamentally unpredictable at that level of detail. A good representation should let you ignore the unpredictable parts and predict the parts that matter: structure, dynamics, what objects will do.

Once I framed it that way, JEPA stopped looking like a competitor to generative models and started looking like a statement about abstraction. Prediction should happen at the right level of abstraction, and you can learn that level instead of hard-coding it as pixels.

I'm still not a JEPA fundamentalist, though. I think the line between generative and joint-embedding methods is getting blurrier. Even in diffusion models, a lot of recent work shows that aligning the internal representations with a good self-supervised encoder helps a lot. That tells me representation learning and generation aren't opposites; they need each other. So my view now is less "JEPA versus generative" and more that the core idea behind JEPA, predicting in a learned abstract space, is probably a necessary ingredient. How exactly it gets implemented is still very much open, and that's what makes it exciting.

r001.rationale: He says JEPA initially felt like “a bit of a repackaging” of existing joint-embedding and self-supervised methods.

r002.rationale: He describes realizing JEPA raises a deeper question about what a world model should capture, and reframes it as a principle of learned abstraction.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that he and his collaborators stopped pursuing self-supervised learning because it was difficult to scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, my first reaction to JEPA was skepticism, and I think a lot of people in the field had the same reaction. When Yann first started talking about it, it felt almost like a philosophical position rather than a concrete method. The idea was that you shouldn't predict pixels, you should predict in a latent space, and the model should learn an abstract representation of the world. And my instinct was, okay, but we've seen so many approaches that look elegant on a whiteboard and then just don't train, or they collapse, or they end up needing so many tricks that the original elegance is gone.

Part of my skepticism also came from my own background. I spent a lot of years on contrastive learning and masked image modeling, and those methods worked because they had very clear signals. With contrastive learning you have positives and negatives, with masked modeling you have reconstruction. JEPA throws away the explicit reconstruction target, and the obvious question is, what stops the encoder from just outputting something trivial? The collapse problem is real, and early on I didn't see a convincing answer that wasn't just another heuristic.

What changed my mind was actually working with it rather than reading about it. A few things happened. First, the empirical results started to come in, with I-JEPA and then V-JEPA, and they weren't just competitive, they were learning something qualitatively different. The representations were more semantic, they captured things like object permanence and dynamics in video without ever being told to care about those things. Second, and this is the part I find more interesting, I started to see the connection to generative models, which is my own area. If you think about diffusion models and representation learning, there's this question of what the model should be modeling. Pixels are a very bad target for understanding. You spend most of your capacity on texture and noise. Predicting in a latent space forces the model to decide what matters, and that's really what we want from a world model.

So I'd say my view went from, this is an idea that sounds nice but won't work, to, this is pointing at the right question even if the current implementations are still early. I don't think JEPA as it exists today is the final answer. There are still issues with how you define the latent space, how you avoid collapse in a principled way, how you scale it. But the underlying claim, that intelligence is about predicting abstract state rather than reconstructing raw inputs, I now take seriously. And I've become more humble about dismissing things just because they don't fit the paradigm I happen to be working in.

r001.rationale: He describes JEPA as initially seeming philosophical rather than concrete and questions whether it would train or avoid collapse. He does not attribute his skepticism to viewing it as merely another self-supervised learning algorithm.

r002.rationale: He says working with JEPA led him to see its connection to generative models and to take seriously its deeper claim about predicting abstract state, showing he came to recognize more in the idea than he initially saw.

r003.rationale: He mentions scaling as an ongoing issue with current implementations, but does not say he and his collaborators stopped pursuing self-supervised learning because it was difficult to scale.

astra-6.text:
Initially, my reaction was: aren’t we already doing something like this with representation learning? You encode one view, predict another representation, and avoid reconstructing every pixel. So I was skeptical about how much of JEPA was a fundamentally new idea versus a different framing of existing ideas.

What I came to appreciate was the question behind it: what should a predictive model actually predict? If you predict pixels, you spend a lot of capacity modeling details that may be unpredictable or irrelevant. Predicting in a representation space gives you a way to focus on something more abstract.

But that also moves the difficult question into the representation itself. What information does it preserve? What can it safely discard? Avoiding collapse doesn’t automatically mean you’ve learned the right abstraction.

So I became more sympathetic to the direction, while still wanting to separate the ambition from what has been demonstrated. I think it’s a useful way to frame the problem. Whether it gives us the kind of world model we ultimately want is still an open question.

r001.rationale: The response says he initially saw JEPA as resembling existing representation-learning ideas, but does not identify it as merely another self-supervised learning algorithm.

r002.rationale: He later appreciates the question of what predictive models should predict and becomes more sympathetic, but does not clearly say JEPA had greater theoretical depth than he initially understood.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention scaling difficulties or that he and his collaborators stopped pursuing a research path for that reason.

sol-6.1.text:
Initially, I was skeptical because I didn’t quite see what made JEPA fundamentally different. You’re predicting a representation instead of pixels—but why should that give you a better understanding of the world? And if the target representation is learned too, how do you know the model isn’t just finding an easy shortcut?

What changed for me was understanding the motivation more clearly. Predicting every pixel forces you to spend capacity on details that may be impossible to predict and irrelevant to the task. If you’re watching someone move behind an object, you care about where they’ll emerge, not the exact texture of their shirt. Predicting in representation space potentially lets you focus on that more meaningful structure.

So I became more sympathetic to the direction. But I’d still separate the principle from any particular implementation. The hard question is what makes the representation preserve the information you’ll actually need. Moving the prediction into latent space doesn’t automatically solve that. My skepticism shifted from ‘Why do this?’ to ‘What makes this work, and how far can it go?’

r001.rationale: The candidate says Xie did not see what made JEPA fundamentally different, but does not describe it as merely another self-supervised learning algorithm.

r002.rationale: The candidate says he understood the motivation more clearly and became more sympathetic, but does not state that he recognized greater theoretical depth.

r003.rationale: The candidate gives no account of Xie and his collaborators stopping that research path or of scaling difficulties as the reason.
